title: Design a Fraud Detection System
summary: The canonical fraud case study, built on extreme class imbalance, delayed ground truth, and an adversary that adapts to you.

slides.markdown:
Fraud detection is a binary classification problem — `fraud` vs `legitimate` — with one defining property: fraud is **rare**, often well under 1% of transactions. This isn't a minor detail, it shapes the entire system: naive training collapses to predicting "legitimate" for everything and still looks 99% accurate (see [handling-imbalanced-data](handling-imbalanced-data) for the general toolkit — resampling, class weighting, threshold moving all apply directly here).

The framing also matters for evaluation: accuracy is meaningless here, and the real conversation is always about precision/recall trade-offs, not a single scalar metric.

Fraud signal lives mostly in **behavioral patterns**, not any single transaction's raw fields:

- **Velocity features** — how many transactions in the last minute/hour/day, sudden spikes vs the user's normal cadence.
- **Graph/network features** — is this card, device, or shipping address linked to other known-fraudulent accounts (fraud rings share infrastructure).
- **Device fingerprinting** — is this the user's usual device, browser, IP geolocation, or a brand-new one appearing minutes after a password reset.

A single $500 purchase means little alone; the same purchase preceded by five failed attempts from three different IPs in two minutes is a very different signal — which is why velocity and graph features usually carry more weight than any static transaction attribute.

Fraud systems typically run **two speeds** at once: a fast, real-time model scores every transaction in milliseconds to make a **block/allow/challenge** decision at checkout, while a slower, heavier batch process re-scores recent transactions with richer features (that take longer to compute) and flags suspicious ones for human review.

The real-time model has to be cheap and simple enough to hit a strict latency SLA; the batch model can afford a much larger feature set and a more expensive ensemble, catching fraud the real-time model missed, just later.

Ground truth for fraud is often confirmed **weeks after the fact** — a chargeback or user dispute is the actual label, and it can take 30-90 days to arrive. This complicates training in a way most other classification problems don't have to deal with: the freshest transactions in your dataset are exactly the ones you don't yet know the true label for.

In practice, this means training data always lags production by the confirmation window, and any "is this model still accurate" question has to account for the fact that recent predictions can't be validated yet at all.

slides.sectionTitle: The precision/recall trade-off in business terms
slides.markdown:
| | High precision (fewer false positives) | High recall (fewer false negatives) |
|---|---|---|
| Business cost | Fewer legitimate customers blocked (false declines) | Fewer actual fraud losses slip through |
| Failure mode | Missed fraud costs money directly | Annoyed/blocked legit customers churn, cost trust |

**How to decide:** the right operating point is set by comparing the dollar cost of a missed fraud case against the cost of a false decline (a frustrated, possibly lost, legitimate customer) — this is a business decision made with the fraud/risk team, not a purely statistical one, and it should be revisited as those relative costs shift.

Fraud detection has an adversary that actively reacts to your model — unlike most ML problems, the underlying data distribution isn't static, it **shifts in direct response** to what you deploy. The moment fraudsters notice a pattern gets blocked, they change tactics; a model that was 95% precise last quarter can quietly degrade because the population it's scoring has adapted around it.

This means fraud models need continuous retraining on fresh data (not a one-time deploy-and-forget), active monitoring for new attack patterns, and often an explicit anomaly-detection layer (see [anomaly-detection](anomaly-detection)) alongside the supervised classifier to catch genuinely novel fraud patterns the classifier has never seen labeled examples of.

slides.subTitle: Setting the threshold from real dollar costs
slides.markdown:
Say an average confirmed fraud case costs the business **$150** (chargeback plus fees), and a false decline costs roughly **$8** in lost margin plus goodwill on a legitimate order. If a candidate threshold would catch 1,000 more fraud cases per month but also decline 25,000 more legitimate orders, the trade is `1,000 x $150 = $150,000` saved against `25,000 x $8 = $200,000` lost — net negative, so that threshold is too aggressive even though it "catches more fraud."

This is the actual math behind "pick the threshold with the risk team" — it's rarely a round number like 0.5, and it should be recomputed whenever the relative costs shift (e.g. holiday season order values rise, changing the false-decline cost).

slides.subTitle: Gradient-boosted trees plus an anomaly layer
slides.markdown:
Most production fraud scorers are **gradient-boosted trees** (XGBoost/LightGBM-style) rather than deep nets — they handle the mix of sparse categorical and dense velocity features well, train fast enough to retrain daily, and their feature importances are easy to explain to a risk analyst reviewing a flagged case (a real operational requirement here, not a nice-to-have).

Alongside the supervised classifier, many systems run an unsupervised **anomaly-detection layer** scoring "how unlike this account's or the population's normal behavior is this" — it catches genuinely novel attack patterns the classifier has never seen a labeled example of, since supervised models can only recognize fraud shaped like fraud they were trained on.

slides.subTitle: Selection bias from only labeling what got flagged
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our labeled training data accurately reflects all the fraud in our transaction stream."

**Why it's wrong:** transactions the model (or a human reviewer) never flagged are usually never investigated, so they default to a "legitimate" label by omission — even if some were actually fraud that simply weren't caught. Training on this data teaches the model to reproduce its own past blind spots, since fraud that historically slipped through never appears as a positive label.

**Correct model:** periodically sample and manually review a random slice of *unflagged* transactions (not just the ones the model already suspected) to estimate the true miss rate and catch this feedback loop before it silently entrenches.
